To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
anxiety and expertise are both important determinants of visual search behaviour in athletes.

(a) the more anxiety-provoking the image, the more peripheral areas are inspected; and (b) the expert riders' actual visual search behaviour did not correspond more closely to their planned search behaviour than the less skilled equestrians.

(a) anxiety is associated with an increase of fixations in peripheral areas of the visual field; (b) anxiety is associated an increase of fixating time on the peripheral area; (c) expert riders allocate more fixations than less skilled riders; and (d) experts are less dependent on overall course plans.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the visual search behaviour and anxiety of athletes.
the relationship between anxiety, strategic visual search behaviour and expertise.
the visual search strategies of athletes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
anxiety is associated with a tendency to look at the environment peripherally, and that the relationship between intended and actual visual search behaviour may not be as strong as has been assumed.
the effects of anxiety and planning on visual search are not clear cut.
, in the case of the equestrian performers, there is a significant relationship between the amount of expertise and the number of fixating points.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the visual search strategies of athletes are not necessarily congruent with their planned strategies and, moreover, that anxiety may have a profound effect on the visual search behaviour that athletes employ.
the effects of anxiety on visual behaviour are not limited to the performance domain.
anxiety is associated with an increased number of fixations in peripheral areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
anxiety can affect the visual search strategies of athletes, but that the relationship is far from simple.

the visual search behaviour that is adopted during sport performance is influenced by the anxiety that athletes feel, and that this behaviour is not necessarily the same as that which athletes plan to adopt.
, contrary to what one might expect, the visual search behaviour and the plans of skilled performers are not always congruent.
